title: Shanghai
description: Municipality and largest city in China
wiki_lead:
Shanghai is a provincial-level direct-administered municipality in China. It has a population of 30,050,000 in the urban area as of 2026, thus making it China's most populous city and the fifth-largest city in the world by population. The city is located on the southern estuary of the Yangtze River, with the Huangpu River bisecting the city.
Shanghai is a global centre for finance, business, research, science and technology, manufacturing, transportation, tourism, and culture. The Port of Shanghai is the world's busiest container port. Separately, the municipality of Shanghai recorded a gross domestic product (GDP) of RMB 5.67 trillion in 2025, representing a year-on-year increase of 5.4%.
Originally a fishing village and market town, Shanghai grew to global prominence in the 19th century due to domestic and foreign trade and its favorable port location. The city was one of five treaty ports forced to open to trade with the Europeans after the First Opium War, with the Shanghai International Settlement and French Concession subsequently established. The city became a primary commercial and financial hub of Asia in the 1930s. During the Second World War, it was the site of the Battle of Shanghai, where it fell under Japanese rule. This was followed by the Chinese Civil War with the Communists taking over the city and most of the mainland. During the Cold War, trade was mostly limited to other socialist countries in the Eastern Bloc, causing the city's global influence to decline.
The reform and opening up supported by Deng Xiaoping led to extensive redevelopment by the 1990s, particularly in the Pudong New Area, spurring the return of finance and foreign investment. The city has re-emerged as a hub for international trade and finance. It is the home of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, the largest stock exchange in the Asia-Pacific by market capitalization and the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, the first free-trade zone in mainland China. It is ranked fifth globally on the Global Financial Centres Index. Shanghai has been classified as an Alpha+ (global first-tier) city by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network. As of 2024, it is home to 13 companies of the Fortune Global 500—the fourth-highest number of any city. Shanghai is the world's second largest city by scientific outputs and home to several highly ranked universities, including Fudan, Shanghai Jiao Tong and Tongji. The Shanghai Metro, first opened in 1993, is the largest metro network in the world by route length.
Shanghai has been described as a global finance and innovation hub, and it is one of the ten biggest economic hubs in the world. Featuring several architectural styles such as Art Deco and shikumen, the city contains the Lujiazui skyline, and museums and historic buildings such as the City God Temple, Yu Garden, the China Pavilion and buildings along the Bund. Shanghai is known for its cuisine, local language, and cosmopolitan culture. It ranks sixth in the list of cities with the most skyscrapers.

Etymology
 The two Chinese characters in the city's name are 上 (Pinyin: shàng; Wugniu: zaon, "upon") and 海 (hǎi; he, "sea"), together meaning "On the Sea". The earliest occurrence of this name is the 11th-century Song dynasty, when there was a river confluence and a town with this name in the area. Others contend that the city is referenced in historical records dating back 2150 years, and that its ancient name, "Hu", suggests it was a fishing village. In 1280 it was renamed "Shanghai", which translates to "Above the Sea". The name's interpretation was disputed, but Chinese historians concluded that during the Tang dynasty, the area of modern-day Shanghai was under sea level, so the land appeared to be "on the sea". The name was also used to refer to Shanghai county (上海县; 上海縣; Shànghǎi Xiàn; zaon-he-yoe), which today has been reorganised into Minhang district.
Shanghai is officially abbreviated 沪 (Traditional: 滬, Hù; wu) in Chinese, a contraction of 沪渎 (滬瀆, Hù
grok_lead: Shanghai is a direct-administered municipality of the People's Republic of China, situated on the southern estuary of the Yangtze River in East China, and ranks as the country's most populous urban area with approximately 30.5 million residents in its metropolitan region as of 2025. It operates as a pivotal global center for finance, international trade, high-technology manufacturing, and maritime shipping, accommodating the Shanghai Stock Exchange âone of the world's largest by trading volumeâand the Port of Shanghai, which handles the highest annual container throughput globally. In 2024, Shanghai's gross domestic product reached 5.39 trillion yuan (approximately 760 billion USD); its nominal GDP per capita in 2025 was US$32,840, underscoring its status as China 's premier economic engine and a key driver of national growth through export-oriented industries and innovation hubs like the Zhangjiang High-Tech Park. Originally a modest fishing village and market settlement dating back over a millennium, Shanghai's transformation into a cosmopolitan metropolis commenced in the 1840s following the Treaty of Nanking, which established foreign concessions that catalyzed infrastructure development, foreign investment, and population influx, peaking in the 1920s-1930s as Asia's preeminent financial hub amid rapid industrialization and cultural efflorescence. After incorporation into the People's Republic in 1949, the city experienced relative economic suppression during central planning eras, marked by ideological campaigns and limited private enterprise, until Deng Xiaoping 's 1978 reforms unleashed market liberalization, special economic zones, and foreign direct investment that propelled exponential GDP growth averaging over 10% annually through the 1990s and 2000s, exemplified by the 1990 designation of Pudong as a development zone fostering iconic skyscrapers and bridging traditional Puxi with futuristic eastern expanses. This trajectory has not been without challenges, including acute wealth disparitiesâevident in a Gini coefficient exceeding 0.4âand environmental strains from unchecked urbanization, though empirical metrics affirm its resilience as a model of state-directed capitalism yielding tangible prosperity gains.
